propositions.text: Dismiss the Minister's appeal against the RPD decision recognizing the Respondents as Convention refugees.
propositions.quote: I dismiss this appeal brought by the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness and the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship.

propositions.text: The RPD correctly found the Respondents were persecuted due to cumulative discrimination based on sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: I find the RPD was correct in finding the Respondents were subjected to cumulative discrimination amounting to persecution due to their sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the Minister's appeal and finds the RPD was correct in recognizing the Respondents as persecuted due to sexual orientation.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Respondents credible and experienced repeated harassment and discrimination forcing them to hide their sexual orientation in China.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Respondents to be credible witnesses. The RPD found credible evidence of the Respondents experiencing repeated harassment, violent aggression and discrimination which compelled the Respondents to hide their sexual orientation in public in order to feel safe from harm in China.

propositions.text: The RPD found the discrimination amounted to persecution when the Respondents lived openly as a lesbian couple in China.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the level of discrimination to amount to persecution when the Respondents lived openly as a lesbian couple in China.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Respondents credible and that discrimination they faced amounted to persecution when living openly as lesbians in China.

propositions.text: The RPD found the state unable and unwilling to protect the Respondents from harassment and discrimination based on sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the state is unable and unwilling to provide protection, and it would be objectively unreasonable for the Respondents to seek state protection for harassment and discrimination in relation to their sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the state unable and unwilling to protect the Respondents from harassment and discrimination.

propositions.text: No Internal Flight Alternatives exist because societal anti-LGBT attitudes are widespread throughout China.
propositions.quote: The societal attitudes towards LGBT persons that caused the Respondents to be targets of repeated harassment and discrimination amounting to persecution are prevalent throughout China.

propositions.text: No laws in China protect the Respondents from anti-LGBT harassment and discrimination.
propositions.quote: There are no laws in place anywhere in China that would protect the Respondents from anti-LGBT harassment and discrimination.

propositions.text: State and police attitudes render state protection ineffective for the LGBT community in China.
propositions.quote: According to the country conditions evidence, the attitudes of the state and the police towards the LGBT community would render state protection ineffective.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no Internal Flight Alternatives due to widespread societal discrimination, lack of protective laws, and ineffective state protection in China.

propositions.text: RAD gave Respondents 30 days to submit new documents or submissions due to COVID-19.
propositions.quote: Due to the coronavirus pandemic, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) provided written notice to the Respondents giving them 30 days to submit new documents or written submissions.

propositions.text: Minister requested extension to file final reply submissions under RAD Rule 11.
propositions.quote: the Minister requested an extension of time to file final reply submissions pursuant to Rule 11 of the RAD Rules.

propositions.text: Extension granted for procedural fairness; Minister filed new evidence and reply after due date but accepted due to valid reason and no time limit for Minister.
propositions.quote: I granted the extension of time on the basis of procedural fairness that the Appellant be given the same opportunity to file new evidence. The Appellant filed new evidence and a final reply submission by August 26, 2020 which was several days after the imposed due date. I accepted the Minister's new evidence and the final written reply because a valid reason was provided, the delay was not inordinate, and the Minister is not subject to any time limits pursuant to Rule 11 in the filing of its reply submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD gave Respondents 30 days to submit documents; Minister requested and was granted extension to file reply submissions, which were accepted despite delay.

propositions.text: Respondents requested to submit new documents and respond to Minister's reply under RAD Rule 29, but attached no new evidence.
propositions.quote: the Respondents made a written request pursuant to Rule 29 of the RAD Rules to submit new documents and to respond to the Appellant's reply with written submissions. No new documents or submissions were attached to the request.

propositions.text: Minister objected to Respondents' request, arguing Minister has right of last reply and allowing Respondents last reply is unfair and a breach of procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: The Appellant objected to the Respondents' request to submit new documents and/or additional written submission, arguing that the Minister has the right of last reply because it is the Appellant, and that allowing the Respondents to have the right of last reply is procedurally unfair, a reviewable error, and a breach of procedural fairness and natural justice.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents requested to submit new documents and reply; Minister objected, claiming right of last reply and procedural unfairness.

propositions.text: Deny Respondents' request to file further evidence and submissions as no new evidence was submitted and to bring finality.
propositions.quote: I deny the Respondents' request to file further evidence and submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court denies Respondents' request to file further evidence and submissions to finalize the procedural process.

propositions.text: Shanghai and Chengdu are viable Internal Flight Alternatives (IFAs).
propositions.quote: Shanghai and Chengdu are viable IFAs.

propositions.text: RPD erred in mixed fact and law by not meaningfully assessing state protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in mixed fact and law in not meaningfully assessing the issue of state protection.

propositions.text: Societal discrimination against LGBTQ persons in China does not amount to persecution.
propositions.quote: Societal discrimination against LGBTQ persons in China does not amount to persecution.

propositions.text: RPD selectively used evidence and ignored positive evidence on societal treatment of LGBTQ persons in China.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in selectively using evidence to support its position, and in ignoring evidence that shed a positive light on the societal treatment of LGBTQ persons in China.

propositions.text: RPD made factual errors regarding incidents of discrimination and harassment.
propositions.quote: The RPD also committed factual errors regarding incidents of discrimination and harassment.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues Shanghai and Chengdu are viable IFAs, RPD erred on state protection, persecution, selective evidence, and factual errors.

propositions.text: Minister submitted country conditions showing China will legislate protection for LGBTQ persons, accepting UN recommendations including banning discrimination within a year.
propositions.quote: the Minister submitted country conditions documents reporting that the Chinese government will legislate protection for LGBTQ persons. China accepted five of the UN Human Rights Council's recommendations on LGBTQ rights in 2019, including the banning of discrimination within a year.

paragraphs.summary: Minister submits China will legislate LGBTQ protections, having accepted UN recommendations including banning discrimination.

propositions.text: Appellant's arguments will be addressed in the analysis section.
propositions.quote: The particulars of the Appellant's arguments will be addressed in the analysis of these reasons for decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court will address the Appellant's arguments in the analysis section.

propositions.text: Discrimination experienced by Respondents amounts to more than a mere possibility of persecution.
propositions.quote: I find the discrimination experienced by the Respondents on account of their sexual orientation give rise to more than a mere possibility of persecution.

propositions.text: No Internal Flight Alternative exists in Shanghai and Chengdu for the Respondents.
propositions.quote: I also find that the Respondents do not have an IFA in Shanghai and Chengdu.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds discrimination amounts to persecution and no Internal Flight Alternative exists in Shanghai or Chengdu.

propositions.text: Dismiss the appeal; RPD was correct in finding Respondents are Convention refugees.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Respondents are Convention refugees.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's finding that the Respondents are Convention refugees.

propositions.text: The RAD standard of review is correctness on questions of law, fact, or mixed fact and law.
propositions.quote: The standard of review at the RAD is correctness on questions of law, fact, or mixed fact and law.

propositions.text: RAD may defer to RPD credibility findings if RPD had meaningful advantage in assessing oral testimony.
propositions.quote: The RAD can defer to an RPD finding where the RPD had a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral testimony.

propositions.text: RAD conducts its own correctness review of the record to determine if RPD erred.
propositions.quote: The RAD carries out its own analysis of the record, on a correctness standard, to determine whether the RPD erred.

propositions.text: The standard of review of this RPD decision is correctness unless otherwise stated.
propositions.quote: Unless otherwise stated, the standard of review of this RPD decision is correctness.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD standard of review is correctness; it may defer to RPD credibility findings but conducts its own analysis.

propositions.text: Appellant argues societal discrimination against LGBTQ persons in China does not amount to persecution.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that societal discrimination against LGBTQ persons in China does not amount to persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues societal discrimination against LGBTQ persons in China does not amount to persecution.

propositions.text: Ward defines persecution as sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights showing failure of state protection.
propositions.quote: The seminal case of Ward defined persecution as the "sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights demonstrative of a failure of state protection".

propositions.text: Federal Court held it is serious interference to hide sexual orientation to avoid punishment; repression is error.
propositions.quote: it is a serious interference with a basic human right to have to hide one's sexual orientation in order to avoid punishment. Accordingly, it is an error to conclude that persecution does not exist because a lesbian couple can live without punishment by hiding their relationship.

propositions.text: Federal Court found it perverse to expect repression of immutable characteristic like sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court has found it is perverse to expect an individual to exercise discretion in expressing their sexual orientation, as it is asking them to repress an immutable characteristic.

propositions.text: SOGIE Guidelines adopt that claimants cannot be expected to conceal sexual orientation to avoid persecution.
propositions.quote: The SOGIE Guidelines adopts this jurisprudence in its guidance that a claimant cannot be expected to conceal their sexual orientation as a way to avoid persecution.

paragraphs.summary: Ward and Federal Court law hold persecution includes forced concealment of sexual orientation; SOGIE Guidelines adopt this principle.

propositions.text: Determining persecution requires assessing cumulative discrimination's effect beyond mere possibility of persecution.
propositions.quote: The determination of whether discrimination rises to the level of persecution requires an assessment of whether the discriminatory actions, viewed as a whole, have a cumulative effect on the claimants, such that the discrimination gives rise to more than a mere possibility of persecution in the minds of the claimants.

propositions.text: Assessment requires contextual approach considering all circumstances creating insecurity and apprehension for claimant.
propositions.quote: The assessment of cumulative discrimination leading to persecution requires a contextual approach that considers all of the circumstances that inform the general atmosphere of insecurity in the country which may give rise to "a feeling of apprehension and insecurity" for the claimant regarding the future.

propositions.text: Assessment considers claimant's individual circumstances and vulnerabilities as factual context.
propositions.quote: The fact-driven assessment considers the claimant's individual circumstances and vulnerabilities, including age, health, and finances as part of the factual context.

propositions.text: Necessary to consider if cumulative past discrimination forms basis of present fear.
propositions.quote: It is necessary to consider whether the cumulative effect of past discriminatory treatment is capable of forming the basis of present fear.

paragraphs.summary: Persecution assessment requires contextual, cumulative discrimination analysis considering claimant's vulnerabilities and present fear.

propositions.text: Preponderance of evidence supports that cumulative discrimination experienced by Respondents gives rise to more than mere possibility of persecution.
propositions.quote: I find the preponderance of evidence supports a finding that the cumulative effects of the discriminatory incidents experienced by the Respondents give rise to more than a mere possibility of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence supports that cumulative discrimination experienced by Respondents amounts to persecution.

propositions.text: No IFA exists in Shanghai and Chengdu because country conditions differ for Chinese LGBT citizens versus visitors or ex-pats.
propositions.quote: I also find that an IFA does not exist in Shanghai and Chengdu because the gist of the articles submitted by the Appellant describe country conditions which visitors and ex-pats travelling in China would encounter, and such country conditions are not the same as those experienced by Chinese citizens who identify as LGBT.

propositions.text: Respondents have established on balance of probabilities they cannot move to Shanghai or Chengdu.
propositions.quote: Additionally, the Respondents have established on a balance of probabilities that they would not be able to move to those cities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no IFA in Shanghai or Chengdu as conditions differ for LGBT Chinese citizens and Respondents cannot move there.

propositions.text: Minister submitted recent country conditions documents about treatment of LGBTQ persons by state and non-state actors.
propositions.quote: The Minister submitted a number of recent developments in the new country conditions documents that fill in the gaps of the current National Documentation Package (NDP) in regards to the treatment of LGBTQ persons by state and non-state actors.

propositions.text: Appellant submitted China will legislate protection for LGBTQ persons after accepting UN recommendations in 2019.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submitted that the Chinese government will legislate protection for LGBTQ persons because China accepted five of the UN Human Rights Council's recommendations on LGBTQ rights in 2019, including the banning of discrimination within a year.

propositions.text: RAD's review shows China has not yet implemented adopted UN recommendations according to Amnesty International.
propositions.quote: The RAD's independent review of the Minister's new country conditions evidence indicates that although China states it has already implemented the recommendations, China has yet to implement the adopted recommendations, according to Amnesty International.

paragraphs.summary: Minister submitted recent country conditions; Appellant says China will legislate protections; RAD finds China has not yet implemented them.

propositions.text: International human rights groups consider China's LGBTQ protections insufficient; employment discrimination persists causing mental health issues.
propositions.quote: The recent country condition evidence submitted by the Minister indicates that international human rights groups still consider China's protection for LGBTQ rights to be insufficient, and that employment discrimination against LGBTQ people continue to persist after coming out of the closet, to the extent that many suffer from mental health problems due to societal pressures.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds international groups consider China's LGBTQ protections insufficient and employment discrimination persists causing mental health problems.

propositions.text: The RPD conducted a thorough and balanced analysis of societal attitudes in China towards LGBTQ people.
propositions.quote: The RPD conducted a thorough and balanced analysis of the societal attitudes in China towards LGBTQ people.

propositions.text: The RPD correctly found lesbians in China are not protected by legislation.
propositions.quote: The RPD is correct that the country conditions support a finding that lesbians in China are not protected by legislation.

propositions.text: The RAD's independent review confirms no legal protections for LGBTQ persons exist in China.
propositions.quote: According to the RAD's independent review, legal protections for LGBTQ persons do not exist in China.

propositions.text: Anti-discrimination laws in China do not cover gender identity or sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: The reach of anti-discrimination laws in China do not address discrimination on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation.

propositions.text: There is no legal right or protection for same-sex partnerships in China.
propositions.quote: There is no legal right or protection for same-sex partnerships in China.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no legal protections for lesbians in China; the RAD independently confirmed no LGBTQ legal protections or rights exist there.

propositions.text: Government policies on LGBTQ issues in China mainly focus on public health.
propositions.quote: Government policies on LGBTQ issues are mainly limited to public health issues.

propositions.text: The government's stance is 'not encouraging, not discouraging, not promoting' LGBTQ persons.
propositions.quote: The stance of the government on LGBTQ persons can be summed up as "not encouraging, not discouraging, not promoting".

propositions.text: This policy is tolerant but does not protect against discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: This policy is one of tolerance but not necessarily of protection against discrimination and harassment on the basis of sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds China's government tolerates LGBTQ persons but does not protect them from discrimination or harassment.

propositions.text: The RAD found some regional governments recognize LGBTQ rights in limited cases.
propositions.quote: The RAD's independent review of the new evidence submitted in the Minister's reply found individual case-by-case examples of a regional government recognizing LGBTQ rights.

propositions.text: Examples include same-sex guardianship in Beijing, Nanjing, Shanghai, Hubei, and others.
propositions.quote: Beijing, Nanjing, Shanghai and Hubei and several other provincial level regions approved cases of same-sex guardianship, whereby a couple becoming each other's guardian grants some of the same benefits conferred by marriage including power of attorney and inheritance rights.

propositions.text: A lesbian partner conceived a child via IVF outside China and registered the child in Beijing with her partner's surname.
propositions.quote: Another example is a partner in a lesbian relationship who was able to conceive a child with a sperm donor through IVF outside of China, and was able to register the child in Beijing, as a single mother, with the child bearing the lesbian's partner's surname.

propositions.text: These examples are too few to show widespread recognition and acceptance of LGBTQ rights in China.
propositions.quote: I find the country conditions evidence citing these examples illustrate how some same-sex couples attain legal rights using existing laws, but such examples are too few to support a finding of wide-spread recognition and acceptance of LGBTQ rights.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found limited regional recognition of LGBTQ rights but not widespread acceptance in China, based on few examples.

propositions.text: LGBTQ organizations have proliferated and attitudes shifted due to government tolerance of non-threatening LGBTQ issues.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that LGBTQ organizations have proliferated, and attitudes toward LGBTQ have shifted because the government is relatively tolerant of LGBTQ issues which do not pose a threat to national security or its political system.

propositions.text: The government's perceived lack of threat explains the relative lack of restrictions on LGBTQ rights movement.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that the perceived lack of a threat is the reason for the relative lack of restrictions on the LGBTQ rights movement, and the relative lack of importance of LGBTQ issues on the government's policy agenda.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues government tolerance of non-threatening LGBTQ issues led to proliferation of LGBTQ organizations and fewer restrictions.

propositions.text: The RAD finds a softer stance on some LGBTQ issues but no widespread recognition of LGBTQ rights in China.
propositions.quote: The RAD's independent review finds that while there is a softer stance on some LGBTQ issues in China, there is no wide-spread recognition of LGBTQ rights.

propositions.text: China's civil code defines marriage as between a man and a woman.
propositions.quote: The new provision in China's civil code continue to define marriage as a union between a man and a woman.

propositions.text: The civil code's 'right to reside' provision may theoretically apply to same-sex couples.
propositions.quote: The new "right to reside" provision in the civil code gives a property owner the power to grant the right to live on the property for a term or for life, which in theory can apply to same-sex couples.

propositions.text: It is unknown if the 'right to reside' provision will provide state protection for same-sex couples.
propositions.quote: According to the country documents submitted by the Minister, it is unknown whether the new civil code provisions on the "right to reside" will provide state protection for same-sex couples.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds no widespread LGBTQ rights recognition; China's civil code defines marriage as heterosexual and uncertain protections for same-sex couples.

propositions.text: The government is ambivalent, not persecutory, toward LGBTQ persons.
propositions.quote: The Minister argued that the government's attitude toward LGBTQ is ambivalence not persecution.

propositions.text: Respondents hide their sexual orientation due to widespread discrimination, not fear of punishment.
propositions.quote: The Minister submitted that there is no evidence that the Respondents are forced to hide their relationship to avoid punishment. Rather, they hide their sexual orientation because of widespread discrimination against LGBTQ persons in China.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues government is ambivalent, not persecutory, and respondents hide orientation due to discrimination, not punishment fear.

propositions.text: Whether respondents face discrimination amounting to persecution based on sexual orientation is the issue.
propositions.quote: Indeed, the issue in this appeal is whether the Respondents face discrimination on the basis of their sexual orientation to the extent of persecution.

propositions.text: Discrimination against LGBTQ persons mainly occurs in family, schools, and workplace.
propositions.quote: The RAD's independent review reveals that the occurrence of discrimination against LGBTQ persons are predominantly in the family, schools, and the workplace.

propositions.text: Common discrimination includes verbal abuse, pressure to change appearance, ostracization, and coercion into heterosexual relationships.
propositions.quote: The most prevalent forms of discrimination include verbal abuse, pressure to modify their appearance, speech and actions, ostracization by teachers and classmates, and coercion by one's family to enter into heterosexual relationships.

propositions.text: Employment discrimination varies from no action to penalties like salary reduction, relocation, probation, and termination.
propositions.quote: The treatment of LGBTQ persons in employment varies, with some employers taking no action to some employers imposing penalties, such as salary reductions, relocation, prolonged probation, and termination of employment.

propositions.text: Most discrimination cases go unreported, including those by public authorities like the Public Security Bureau.
propositions.quote: The majority of cases of discrimination against LGBTQ persons go unreported, including discrimination from public authorities such as the Public Security Bureau.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies discrimination against LGBTQ persons mainly in family, school, and work, often unreported, raising the persecution issue.

propositions.text: Government monitoring of LGBTQ groups is part of a general trend affecting all NGOs.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also argued that the government's attitude toward LGBTQ people does not amount to persecution because the risk of persecution for LGBTQ people is a generalized risk. For instance, the increase in the government's monitoring of LGBTQ groups is not unique to LGBTQ organizations but is an overall trend applicable to all NGOs;

propositions.text: The social credit system applies to all Chinese citizens, not just LGBTQ persons.
propositions.quote: the social credit system applies to all Chinese citizens;

propositions.text: Banning LGBTQ depictions on TV and internet is general censorship, not targeted persecution.
propositions.quote: and the banning of LGBTQ depictions on TV and internet is a general act of censorship laws.

propositions.text: The court rejects these arguments, finding discrimination specific to respondents establishes nexus to Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by these arguments: the Respondents are seeking refugee protection because they allege to have experienced discrimination specific to them in the form of physical and verbal threats on account of their sexual orientation, and that they have not been given adequate state protection.

propositions.text: Other groups facing monitoring or harassment does not make the risk generalized.
propositions.quote: The fact that other identifiable groups also face monitoring or harassment does not make any of it a generalized risk.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues persecution risk is generalized; the court rejects this, finding specific discrimination against respondents.

propositions.text: The court disagrees with the Minister that respondents faced only vandalism and no repeated violence due to sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the Minister's argument that the Respondents have not faced repeated violence acts of aggression due to their sexual orientation, and that they have only been subjected to an act of vandalism against property and an act of aggression against themselves.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with the Minister that respondents faced only vandalism and no repeated violence due to sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Two vandalism incidents at Principal Respondent's store are discriminatory acts contributing to persecution finding.
propositions.quote: I find the two occurrences of the Principal Respondent's store being vandalized are acts of discrimination that contributed to the finding of persecution.

propositions.text: The vandalism was motivated by discrimination based on sexual orientation, linked to a customer's homophobic remarks.
propositions.quote: The Principal Respondent testified to her belief that the vandalism was linked to a customer who had previously made homophobic remarks at the store.

propositions.text: The police took no action after the vandalism reports, ignoring surveillance video and complaint.
propositions.quote: The police took no action after she reported the crimes. The police ignored the surveillance video and did not investigate the complaint.

propositions.text: Police inaction caused the Principal Respondent to close the store.
propositions.quote: The inaction of the police caused her to close down the store.

propositions.text: The court rejects the Minister's argument that the vandalism motive is speculative, finding evidence links it to hate crime.
propositions.quote: I do not accept the Minister's argument that it is speculative that the vandalism was motivated by discrimination based on sexual orientation, as there is evidence to link the vandalism to a hate crime based on sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds vandalism of the Principal Respondent's store was a hate crime linked to homophobic remarks; police ignored reports causing closure.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by speculating vandalism was a hate crime without clear evidence of the perpetrator.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that the RPD erred in speculating that the vandalism was a hate crime when the evidence is unclear as to who committed it.

propositions.text: The court rejects the appellant's argument that police inaction relates only to state protection issue.
propositions.quote: I do not accept the Appellant's argument that the inaction of the police to assess the surveillance footage is only relevant to the issue of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues vandalism was speculative hate crime; the court rejects this and appellant's view on police inaction relevance.

propositions.text: The RPD found verbal harassment, vandalism, and police inaction created a chain causing respondents to feel unsafe and targeted.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the evidence of the verbal harassment from a customer, the vandalism targeting only her store, and the police inaction as a chain of events that led the Respondents to feel unsafe and that exposed her be further targeted.

propositions.text: The RPD accepted the Principal Respondent's testimony as truthful with no credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The RPD was correct to accept the Principal Respondent's testimony as truthful, as the RAD's independent review found no negative credibility concerns.

propositions.text: The RPD accepted the belief that homophobic remarks linked to vandalism ignored by police.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RPD was correct to accept the Respondents' belief that the homophobic remarks were linked to the vandalism of the store, which the police ignored when the Principal Respondent reported the incidents.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found harassment, vandalism, and police inaction caused respondents to feel unsafe; accepted testimony and belief linking remarks to vandalism.

propositions.text: The Associate Respondent was told by a police academy tutor to hide her sexual orientation to become a police officer.
propositions.quote: A tutor from the police training academy pulled the Associate Respondent aside and told her to hide her sexual orientation if she desires to become a police officer.

propositions.text: The appellant correctly notes no official prevented completion of police training.
propositions.quote: Although the Appellant is correct to point out that neither the academy or any official from the academy prevented her from completing the training,

propositions.text: The incident caused the Associate Respondent to quit police training due to pressure to choose between career and sexual orientation expression.
propositions.quote: the incident caused the Associate Respondent to quit her police academy training because she felt pressured to choose between being a police officer and being able to express her sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Pressure to hide sexual orientation is discrimination in education and employment, adding to cumulative persecution.
propositions.quote: This pressure to hide her sexual orientation is a form of discrimination, in the education and employment domains, that adds to cumulative discrimination amounting to persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The Associate Respondent was pressured to hide orientation in police training, causing her to quit; this is discrimination adding to persecution.

propositions.text: The Principal Respondent experienced workplace and police discrimination based on sexual orientation.
propositions.quote: I find the Principal Respondent experienced discrimination in her workplace and by the police on the basis of her sexual orientation.

propositions.text: The Principal Respondent fought back a co-worker who made offensive sexual orientation comments and attempted to kiss or attack the Associate Respondent.
propositions.quote: The Principal Respondent was involved in an altercation when she fought back a co-worker who made offensive comments related to her sexual orientation and then attempted either to kiss or attack the Associate Respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Respondent faced workplace and police discrimination, including an altercation with a co-worker making offensive sexual orientation comments.

propositions.text: The Principal Respondent identified the co-worker who assaulted them in photographs and testified about the assault's motivation.
propositions.quote: The Principal Respondent identified the co-worker who assaulted them in the photographs. The Principal Respondent testified that the co-worker in the photographs assaulted the Associate Respondent while using foul language to admonish the Respondents for dressing like a man or boy and for liking girls.

propositions.text: The Minister argues the assault's motivation is unclear.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by the Minister's argument that the motivation behind the work altercation is unclear.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Respondent identified the co-worker and testified assault was motivated by sexual orientation; the Minister disputes motivation clarity.

propositions.text: It is immaterial whether the co-worker was brought to police; relevant is discriminatory police treatment before release.
propositions.quote: Contrary to the Minister's argument, I find it is immaterial whether or not the co-worker who assaulted the Respondent was brought to the police. What is relevant is the discriminatory treatment against the Principal Respondent at the police station before she was released with a warning after being detained for six hours.

propositions.text: Police told the Principal Respondent she was not 'normal' and warned against openness about sexual orientation with threats of greater consequences.
propositions.quote: The police officer told the Principal Respondent that she was not "normal", warned her not to be so open about her sexual orientation, and that if they continued to be open about their relationship, there would be greater consequences.

propositions.text: The Principal Respondent remained silent during police reprimand to avoid dissent.
propositions.quote: She remained silent during this reprimand as she did not want to dissent with the police.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds police discriminated against the Principal Respondent with threats over sexual orientation openness; silence was chosen to avoid dissent.

propositions.text: After the altercation, the Principal Respondent was told not to return to work by employer.
propositions.quote: After the altercation, the Principal Respondent was told by her employer not to return to work.

propositions.text: The Associate Respondent quit the same employer after the Principal Respondent's termination.
propositions.quote: This termination prompted the Associate Respondent to terminate her employment with the same employer.

propositions.text: The Principal Respondent was terminated due to prominent display of sexual orientation, seen as 'abnormal' by employer.
propositions.quote: The Principal Respondent testified that she was terminated because she displayed her sexual orientation more prominently in her appearance; hence, it was more convenient for the employer to let go of an "abnormal" employee.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Respondent was terminated for openly displaying sexual orientation; the Associate Respondent quit the same employer.

propositions.text: The Minister argues termination could be due to physical altercation.
propositions.quote: The Minister has a valid argument that the Principal Respondent could have been terminated due to the physical altercation.

propositions.text: Lack of clarity on termination reason does not negate discrimination based on sexual orientation in workplace.
propositions.quote: However, the lack of clarity as to the reasons for the termination does not mean that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation did not exist in the Respondents' workplace because it is clear from the testimony that the co-worker's assault against the Associate Respondent was motivated by his dislike of the Respondents' sexual orientation and of their external appearances that did not conform with the co-worker's expectations for their gender.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues termination may be due to altercation; court finds unclear reasons do not negate sexual orientation discrimination in workplace.

propositions.text: The court accepts that the Principal Respondent's 'boyish' appearance was a factor in employment termination.
propositions.quote: After consideration of the testimony and the country conditions evidence about employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, I accept the Respondent's assertion that her appearance as a "boyish looking female" was one consideration underlying the termination of employment.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts the Principal Respondent's boyish appearance contributed to her employment termination.

propositions.text: The appellant argues the RPD did not meaningfully assess state protection issue.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that the RPD did not meaningfully assess the issue of state protection.

propositions.text: The court finds merit in appellant's argument that RPD's state protection reasoning could be more thorough.
propositions.quote: This argument has merit in so far as the RPD's reasoning on state protection could have been more fulsome by examining whether the Respondents made reasonable efforts to exhaust all courses of action to access state protection, or whether there was a compelling reason for not doing so.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues RPD inadequately assessed state protection; the court agrees the reasoning could be more thorough.

propositions.text: There is adequate state protection as no evidence shows state, police, or judiciary failed lesbians facing assault or harassment.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that there is adequate state protection because there is no evidence that the state, the police, or the judiciary failed to protect lesbians who are physically assaulted or harassed on the basis of sexual orientation

propositions.text: Disagrees with the appellant's arguments about adequate state protection and recourse for lesbians.
propositions.quote: I disagree with both of these arguments.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues adequate state protection exists for assaulted lesbians; the court disagrees with these arguments.

propositions.text: Respondents rebutted presumption of state protection due to police inaction and discriminatory conduct.
propositions.quote: The Respondents have rebutted the presumption of state protection. The preponderance of evidence indicates that state protection does not exist given the police inaction to the hate crime complaint, the discriminatory reprimand made by the police when the Respondents were taken to the police station, and the discriminatory remarks at the police academy to hide the Associate Respondent's sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents rebutted presumption of state protection citing police inaction and discrimination, as the court notes.

propositions.text: Adequate state protection depends on claimants' ability to access protection at operational level; perfection not required; serious efforts expected unless compelling reason.
propositions.quote: The determination of whether there is adequate state protection turns on whether the claimants' efforts to access state protection would result in adequate state protection at the operational level. State protection does not need to rise to a standard of perfection. A person is expected to make serious efforts to identify and to access state protection, unless there is a compelling or persuasive reason to refrain from doing so.

paragraphs.summary: Court states adequate state protection depends on operational access; perfection not required; serious efforts expected unless compelling reason.

propositions.text: SOGIE Guidelines guide assessment; absence of criminalizing laws does not mean no discrimination or state protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD's independent assessment is guided by the SOGIE Guidelines, in particular that the absence of laws that criminalize or discriminate against LGBTQ individuals does not signify a lack of discrimination or the availability of state protection.

propositions.text: Homosexuality decriminalized in 1997; sex between women never criminalized in China.
propositions.quote: Although homosexuality was decriminalized in 1997, and sex between women was never criminalized

propositions.text: Absence of criminalizing laws does not signify availability of state protection for harm linked to sexual orientation discrimination.
propositions.quote: the absence of laws that criminalize or discriminate against LGBTQ individuals do not signify the availability of state protection for harm linked to discrimination based on sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains SOGIE Guidelines and that absence of criminal laws does not mean state protection exists for LGBTQ harm.

propositions.text: RPD erred by importing Canadian standard equating China's non-recognition of same-sex partnerships to persecution.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that the RPD erroneously imported a Canadian standard to arrive at its conclusion that China's non-recognition of same-sex partnerships is tantamount to persecution or harm.

propositions.text: Rejects appellant's argument; respondents seek protection due to threats and lack of state protection, not marriage recognition.
propositions.quote: I am not swayed by this argument because the Respondents are not seeking protection merely because they are unable to legally marry or to have their union recognized in China. Rather, the Respondents are seeking refugee protection because they felt the need to hide their sexual orientation, due to physical and verbal threats and animosity against them on account of their sexual orientation, and felt that they had no access to state protection.

propositions.text: Respondents' fear linked to vandalism, discriminatory co-worker actions, police inaction, and police discriminatory remarks.
propositions.quote: The Respondents' subjective fear of a threat to their safety can be traced to the vandalism at the store, the discriminatory actions of their co-workers, the inactions of the police, and the discriminatory remarks by the police.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues RPD erred by applying Canadian standard; court rejects, noting respondents' fear stems from threats and lack of protection.

propositions.text: Appellant cites successful Chinese lawsuits against unfair treatment based on employment, consumer protection, and health laws.
propositions.quote: The Appellant cited several successful lawsuits in China for unfair treatment based on existing laws related to employment, consumer protection and health services.

propositions.text: Successful litigation relates to specific legislated areas; some cases unsuccessful; media coverage shows advocacy efforts.
propositions.quote: The examples of litigation for recourse against discrimination based on sexual orientation speak to the treatment of such litigants within the context of those legislated areas. The same article indicates that some litigation cases against LGBTQ discrimination were unsuccessful. These lawsuits were covered in the media to illustrate the advocacy efforts used to raise awareness of the LGBTQ movement in China.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant cites successful lawsuits on unfair treatment; court finds these relate to specific areas with mixed success and advocacy coverage.

propositions.text: Successful litigation cases are limited, mixed in results, unrelated to police discrimination; cannot show broad state protection availability.
propositions.quote: Given the small sample of cases covered in the media article, the mixed results of the litigation efforts of the LGBTQ community, and that none of the litigation cases relate to the police for discriminatory actions or inaction, I find the successful litigation speaks specifically to the factual situations confined to those cases. Although it may demonstrate some progress in employment, consumer protection and health services, the successful litigation cannot be extrapolated into a broader generalized finding that adequate state protection is available from the police to protect the Respondents from the discrimination and harassment they experienced on account of their sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds successful litigation limited, mixed, unrelated to police, and insufficient to show broad state protection.

propositions.text: Respondents rebutted presumption of state protection; police inaction and discriminatory remarks occurred.
propositions.quote: I uphold the RPD finding that the Respondents have rebutted the presumption of state protection. The Respondents first tested the ability of the state to protect them when they filed a police complaint about the vandalism, and they were met with police inaction. In their next interaction with the police after the altercation with the co-worker, the police reprimanded the Principal Respondent with discriminatory remarks. The Associate Respondent experienced discrimination when she was told to hide her sexual orientation at the police training academy.

propositions.text: Discriminatory police conduct justifies refraining from further attempts to access state protection.
propositions.quote: The discrimination exhibited by the police and by the police training academy during the Respondents' interaction with them is a compelling and persuasive reason for refraining from further attempts to access state protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court upholds RPD finding that respondents rebutted state protection presumption due to police discrimination and inaction.

propositions.text: RPD correctly found state protection would not be forthcoming and seeking it would be unreasonable if respondents returned to China.
propositions.quote: Hence, the RPD was correct to find that state protection would not be forthcoming. The RPD was correct in finding that if the Respondents were to return to China, it would not be objectively reasonable for them to seek state protection for any incidents of harassment and discrimination related to sexual orientation.

paragraphs.summary: RPD correctly found state protection unavailable and seeking it unreasonable if respondents returned to China.

propositions.text: Assigns no weight to Hong Kong court cases cited by appellant due to Hong Kong's judicial independence from Mainland China.
propositions.quote: I assign no weight to the court cases from Hong Kong that are cited by the Appellant. Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of China that is given a high degree of autonomy under the "one country, two systems" framework, with the exception of defense and foreign affairs. Hence, the Hong Kong judiciary is independent of the judiciary in Mainland China.

paragraphs.summary: Court assigns no weight to Hong Kong cases cited by appellant due to judicial independence from Mainland China.

propositions.text: No evidence physical altercation prevented respondents from relocating in China; NDP shows legal relocation possible despite Hukou system.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that there is no evidence that the physical altercation prevented the Respondents from relocating in China, and the NDP indicates it is possible to legally relocate in China despite the Hukou registration system as evidenced by the millions who have done so.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues no evidence physical altercation prevented relocation; NDP shows legal relocation possible despite Hukou.

propositions.text: RPD ignored articles about Shanghai and Chengdu as IFAs where respondents can live openly without risk.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argued that the RPD ignored articles about Shanghai and Chengdu being IFAs where the Respondents can live openly as a couple without risk.

propositions.text: Agrees RPD should have explained why appellant's articles on Shanghai and Chengdu were not given greater weight; unclear if ignored or considered.
propositions.quote: I agree with the argument to the extent that the RPD should have explained why the Appellant's articles were not assigned greater weight in the consideration of Shanghai and Chengdu as IFAs. As the RPD was silent on the articles about Shanghai and Chengdu, I cannot ascertain whether the RPD indeed ignored the articles or whether the RPD considered the articles but did not write about them.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues RPD ignored articles on Shanghai and Chengdu as IFAs; court agrees RPD should have explained weight given.

propositions.text: Respondents have no internal flight alternative in China; cannot live openly as lesbians anywhere; would suffer serious human rights interference.
propositions.quote: Based on an independent review of the evidence, I uphold the RPD finding that the Respondents have no IFA in China as they would not be able to live openly as lesbians anywhere in China, and therefore, they would suffer a serious interference with their basic human rights.

paragraphs.summary: Court upholds RPD finding no internal flight alternative; respondents cannot live openly as lesbians in China.

propositions.text: Onus on claimant to show serious possibility of persecution throughout country including IFAs; test includes objective reasonableness to relocate before seeking refuge abroad.
propositions.quote: The onus of proof is on the claimant to demonstrate a serious possibility of persecution throughout the country, including the areas identified as the IFA. The RPD correctly cited the test for IFA: a. The claimant must demonstrate a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA. b. The second prong of the test asks whether it is objectively reasonable to expect the claimant to seek safety in another part of the country before seeking refuge elsewhere. In other words, would it be unduly harsh to expect this person, who is being persecuted in one part of the country, to move to another part of the country before seeking refugee status abroad.

paragraphs.summary: RPD correctly cited IFA test: claimant must show persecution possibility and objective reasonableness to relocate before seeking refuge abroad.

propositions.text: Respondents' hukous are a barrier to relocation; Associate Respondent testified no property ownership in Shanghai or Chengdu.
propositions.quote: The testimony and the objective evidence support a finding, on a balance of probabilities, that the Respondents' hukous are a barrier to their relocation to Shanghai or Chengdu. The Associate Respondent testified that she would not be able to relocate because she owns no property in Shanghai or Chengdu which would entitle her to live there.

propositions.text: Hukou system regulates internal migration; reforms marginally weakened it; legal migration requires local government permission; undocumented migrants lack legal work and social benefits.
propositions.quote: This testimony is supported by the country conditions evidence that the hukou system regulates the internal migration of Chinese citizens from one locale to another. The hukou designates the location where the person may legally reside on a permanent basis and have access to that locale's community-based rights, opportunities, benefits, services, and privileges. Reforms in the hukou system in the 2001 and 2005 have had a marginal impact on the weakening of the system. Permission to legally migrate to a different city outside of the hukou is determined by the government in the locality and can be based on the migrant's exchange of highly skilled talent or investments. Undocumented migrants without hukou authorization are not legally permitted to work. Although undocumented migrants work in the informal sector, they are excluded from access to social security, health insurance, and education, or they must pay higher prices for such services.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found hukou system and lack of property ownership bar respondents' relocation to Shanghai or Chengdu.

propositions.text: Minister's evidence not addressed by RPD; travel articles insufficient to prove ability to live openly or state protection in Shanghai or Chengdu.
propositions.quote: Even considering the Minister's evidence, which the RPD did not address, it would not be reasonable to expect the Respondents to move to Shanghai or Chengdu which were proposed as IFAs. Although the travel articles suggest that a LGBTQ community exists in Shanghai and Chengdu, the articles are not sufficiently probative of the ability of Chinese citizens to live in those cities and to express one's sexual orientation freely without interference with their basic human rights. Nor do the articles address the availability of state protection for discrimination and harassment against Chinese citizens who are LGBTQ in Shanghai and Chengdu.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds travel articles insufficient to prove respondents can live openly or have state protection in Shanghai or Chengdu.

propositions.text: Appellant's articles target travelers and expats; less weight assigned compared to objective country evidence in NDP.
propositions.quote: The gist of the Appellant's articles is to provide information about the public culture and services available in Shanghai and Chengdu for travellers and ex-pats in the LGBTQ community. Written in English, these articles speak to the intended audience of travellers or expats in China. Therefore, I assign less weight to the articles when assessed in conjunction with the objective country evidence found in the NDP.

paragraphs.summary: Court assigns less weight to appellant's articles aimed at travelers and expats compared to objective country evidence.

propositions.text: Wikipedia page describes LGBTQ venues and events in Shanghai; notes puritanical societal views but tolerance for gay and lesbian travelers.
propositions.quote: The Wikipedia page on "LGBTQ culture in Shanghai" describes a number of food and entertainment venues, community hubs, and a LGBTQ Tourism Week. The Wikipedia page sums up the attitude towards sexual orientation with a quote from a well-known travel guide: "Chinese society sees all sexual relations in a puritanical manner, so Shanghai does not have specialized LGBTQ resources;" however "Shanghai is quite tolerant of gay and lesbian travelers."

paragraphs.summary: Wikipedia describes LGBTQ venues and events in Shanghai, noting societal puritanism but tolerance for gay and lesbian travelers.

propositions.text: Article states Shanghai is best place for LGBTQ in China with nightlife and venues; notes family disapproval and limited acceptance.
propositions.quote: Another article states in its preface: "Although Shanghai still has some way to go before being gay is totally acceptable, it is almost certainly the best place to be if you identify as LGBTQ in China." The article goes on to describe Shanghai's gay nightlife, with examples of some food and drinking establishments. The article acknowledges that "while being out and proud may be growing more acceptable with every year that passes" there is general disapproval of gay and lesbian relationships by family members. The article suggests a dance hall as "is the only place where they can truly be themselves".

paragraphs.summary: Article describes Shanghai as best place for LGBTQ in China with nightlife but notes family disapproval and limited acceptance.

propositions.text: Article by Utopia Asia describes Shanghai as best for LGBTQ with venues and festivals; written for tourists and foreigners.
propositions.quote: A similar tenor runs throughout the article "Gay Shanghai, Chinese Gay and Lesbian Resources in China" by Utopia Asia. This article states that Shanghai is the best place for LGBTQ people in respect to the numerous venues and festivals listed. This article was written for tourists or foreigners as it includes tour guides operating in English.

paragraphs.summary: Utopia Asia article describes Shanghai as best for LGBTQ with venues and festivals, aimed at tourists and foreigners.

propositions.text: Articles show Shanghai's LGBTQ culture makes it more progressive for travellers and expats.
propositions.quote: The articles are evidence that the existence of a LGBTQ culture in Shanghai makes the city more progressive for LGBTQ travellers and expats.

propositions.text: Articles do not show Chinese residents in Shanghai can freely express sexual orientation without repercussions.
propositions.quote: The articles do not indicate that Chinese residents of Shanghai can freely and openly express their sexual orientation without repercussions in their daily lives within their families, and in the public institutions of schools and the workplace.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds articles show Shanghai is progressive for LGBTQ travellers but not for Chinese residents to express orientation freely.

propositions.text: Minister argues Respondents can live openly in Chengdu based on submitted articles.
propositions.quote: I have considered the Minister's argument that the Respondents can live openly in Chengdu, based on the articles submitted.

propositions.text: Conde Nast Traveler article describes Chengdu as home to a vibrant and visible lesbian community.
propositions.quote: An article published by Conde Nast Traveler describes Chengdu as a home to "a vibrant and visible lesbian community".

propositions.text: First widely reported gay and lesbian weddings occurred in Chengdu but are not legal marriages.
propositions.quote: The first widely reported gay marriage and the first high-profile lesbian wedding occurred in Chengdu. However, I note that these are wedding ceremonies and not legal marriages, as same-sex marriage is not legally recognized in China, as acknowledged by the article.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Minister's argument and articles describing Chengdu's visible lesbian community and non-legal same-sex weddings.

propositions.text: Conde Nast Traveler article gives anecdotal evidence of more openly gay residents in Chengdu.
propositions.quote: The Conde Nast Traveler article contains anecdotal evidence of a higher proportion of local residents who openly identify as gay or lesbian: gay Chinese couples can hold hands openly without judgment; an openly gay professor was quoted that "Everybody in China knows that Chengdu is a very famous gay city. It's much easier to be gay here than in Shanghai or Beijing."

propositions.text: Chengdu's accepting culture linked to its history as a melting pot from 17th century resettlement.
propositions.quote: An explanation for the more accepting culture is that Chengdu was the capital of a rebel kingdom in the 17th century, which became uninhabited. When citizens were ordered to re-inhabit the city, a "melting pot atmosphere" welcomed and assimilated anyone. An outsider culture became part of the local identity.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the article's anecdotal evidence of Chengdu's gay openness and historical reasons for its accepting culture.

propositions.text: Conde Nast article's anecdotal evidence is aimed at tourists and expats, less weight for assessing state protection for residents.
propositions.quote: Since the intended audience of the Conde Nast Traveler article is tourists and ex-pats, the quote from the openly gay Chinese professor in Chengdu is information for tourists and ex-pats on the LGBTQ culture they may encounter during their visit. Such anecdotal evidence for non-citizens carries less weight for assessing whether the Respondents will be afforded state protection or the freedom to express their sexual orientation openly if they live in Chengdu.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the article's anecdotal evidence less weighty for assessing state protection for residents.

propositions.text: Another travel article describes Chengdu as tolerant and gay people as 'invisible' blending in socially.
propositions.quote: In another travel article, Chengdu is described as a city where being gay is "tolerated" and one can "blend in" to the point that gay-only bars are not necessary. The quotes are from Chinese gay people who describe themselves as "invisible" because there are clubs and restaurants where they can socialize in groups with their women and straight friends.

propositions.text: This article must be assessed as travel writing for tourists on gay culture venues.
propositions.quote: This article must be assessed in the context of travel writing that provides information on gay culture, including a list of bars and clubs, where tourists can go to participate in LGBTQ culture.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes another travel article describes Chengdu's gay tolerance but is aimed at tourists and ex-pats.

propositions.text: Two Chengdu organizations serve LGBTQ community but insufficient to conclude freedom or state protection for lesbian couple.
propositions.quote: There are two organizations in Chengdu that offer services to the LGBTQ community in the Chinese language. However, the existence of these two organizations is insufficient to conclude that the Respondents will be able to work or study freely and openly as a lesbian couple in Chengdu, or that state protection exists in Chengdu to protect against harassment and discrimination at work and school.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds two Chengdu LGBTQ organizations insufficient to prove freedom or state protection for lesbian couples.

propositions.text: Anecdotal quotes suggest greater public tolerance in Chengdu but little objective data on open living or state protection for LGBTQ citizens.
propositions.quote: The small sample of anecdotal quotations in these articles suggest a greater tolerance by the general public for the LGBTQ community in Chengdu than in other cities in China. Other than anecdotal quotations, these articles provide little objective data on whether LGBTQ people who are Chinese citizens in Chengdu and not ex-pats and visitors, can live openly while participating in school or the workforce. The articles provide little objective data on whether LGBTQ Chinese citizens in Chengdu will be afforded state protection against harassment and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

propositions.text: Assign less weight to these articles within the factual matrix of country conditions evidence in the NDP.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I assign less weight to the articles when they are assessed within the factual matrix of the country conditions evidence found in the NDP.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds little objective data on open living or state protection for LGBTQ citizens in Chengdu and assigns less weight to these articles.

propositions.text: Given diminished weight to articles about Shanghai and Chengdu, IFAs are not reasonable in all circumstances.
propositions.quote: Given the diminished weight assigned to the articles about Shanghai and Chengdu, I find the IFAs are not reasonable in all the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the IFAs are not reasonable given diminished weight to articles about Shanghai and Chengdu.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed; RPD was correct in finding Respondents are Convention refugees.
propositions.quote: The appeal is dismissed. The RPD was correct in finding that the Respondents are Convention refugees.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and upholds the RPD's finding that Respondents are Convention refugees.
